sourceEvidence:
SOURCE 1 — The Hollywood Hills session (The Doors of Perception, Huxley, 1954):
Huxley describes seeing a vase of flowers: "I was seeing what Adam had seen on the morning of his creation—the miracle, moment by moment, of naked existence."
He describes going into the garden: "…a Last Judgment which, after a long time and with considerable difficulty, I recognized as a chair."

SOURCE 2 — On the coining of "psychedelic" (Marlan, Beyond Cannabis, 2019):
"The term 'psychedelic' was coined by psychiatric researcher Humphry Osmond. Osmond combined the Greek words psyche ('mind' or 'soul') with delein ('to make manifest') to create a new word meaning 'mind manifesting.' Osmond's aim was to describe a class of substances that catalyze the emergence into conscious awareness of previously unconscious or repressed cognitions, perceptions, and emotions."

SOURCE 3 — On Osmond's Saskatchewan work (Cambridge HPS dissertation, 2007):
"Humphrey Osmond and John Smythies studied mescaline in London and concluded that the outward symptoms of mescaline intoxication were similar to those of schizophrenia. In 1952, Osmond pointed out the structural similarity between mescaline and adrenaline and hypothesised that schizophrenia might have a biochemical basis. Osmond moved to Saskatchewan in Canada to continue his investigations and met Abram Hoffer — through their collaboration they realised that psychedelic drugs had great medical potential. After experimenting with LSD they noticed that the drug often provided patients with personal insights and clear self-reflection and, by 1953, they theorised that it could be used to treat chronic alcoholism."

SOURCE 4 — The naming competition:
Huxley's losing verse: "To make this trivial world sublime, take half a gramme of phanerothyme."
Osmond's winning verse: "To fathom Hell or go angelic, just take a pinch of psychedelic."
The word appeared in print for the first time in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences in 1957.

SOURCE 5 — The MK-Ultra context (Drug Science, LSD History & Law, 2021):
"April 13, 1953: CIA Director Allen Dulles signs the MK-Ultra authorization memorandum. The program would test LSD and other substances on unwitting subjects. May 3, 1953: Osmond administers mescaline to Huxley in Hollywood Hills. The two projects — one therapeutic, one weaponized — begin within three weeks of each other."

sourceEvidence:
SOURCE 1 — Hofmann's account of April 16-19, 1943 (LSD: My Problem Child, 1979):
"In the afternoon of 16 April 1943, when I was working on this problem, I was seized by a peculiar sensation of vertigo and restlessness. Objects, as well as the shape of my associates in the laboratory, appeared to undergo optical changes. I was unable to concentrate on my work. In a dreamlike state I left for home, where an irresistible urge to lie down overcame me. I sank into a not unpleasant, intoxicated condition characterized by an extremely stimulated imagination. In a dreamlike state, with eyes closed, I perceived an uninterrupted stream of fantastic pictures, extraordinary shapes with intense, kaleidoscopic play of—" [entry ends here]

April 19: "On 19 April 1943, I carried out a self-experiment with 0.25 mg of LSD. I had estimated that this amount was so small that it would be harmless."
"My field of vision swayed before me, and objects appeared distorted like images in curved mirrors. I had the impression of being unable to move from the spot, although my assistant told me later that we had cycled at a good pace."
The neighbor: "A female neighbor, whom I scarcely recognized, brought me milk — she had become a malevolent, insidious witch with a colored mask."
The morning after (Hofmann, LSD: My Problem Child, chapter 1): "…everything glistened and sparkled in a fresh light. The world was as if newly created."

SOURCE 2 — The pharmacology (Nichols, Pharmacological Reviews, 2016):
"The primary mechanism of action of the psychedelic drugs is as agonists or partial agonists at the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor. LSD binds with exceptional affinity to 5-HT2A receptors. The drug's action at the thalamus, which serves as the primary sensory gating mechanism, may explain the characteristic alteration in sensory experience. The dose Hofmann administered to himself (0.25 mg) is approximately 2.5 times what modern clinical trials use as a full therapeutic dose."

SOURCE 3 — The historical context (Cambridge HPS dissertation, 2007):
"By the mid 1960s, over 40,000 patients had taken LSD and psychedelic research had produced over 1,000 scientific papers and many books as well as several international conferences. LSD was made illegal in the US in 1968. The research stopped."

sourceEvidence:
SOURCE 1 — The initiates' testimony (classical sources):
Sophocles: "Thrice happy are those mortals who see these rites before they depart to Hades; for to them alone is it granted to have true life there; to the rest all there is evil."
Cicero: "Athens has given nothing to the world more excellent or divine than the Eleusinian Mysteries. We have learned from them the beginnings of life, and have gained the power not only to live happily, but also to die with a better hope."
Pindar (as translated by Nilsson): "he knows the end of life and he knows its god-sent beginning."

SOURCE 2 — Wasson on the kykeon (The Road to Eleusis, 1978):
"The kykeon, this simple drink of water, mint, and barley... We believe that the barley was parasitized by ergot, and that the ergotized barley was the active principle of the kykeon. Ergot contains ergine (d-lysergic acid amide) and other psychoactive alkaloids."

SOURCE 3 — Hofmann on the chemistry (The Road to Eleusis, 1978):
"I carried out a self-experiment with ergonovine, a water-soluble ergot alkaloid. After ingesting 0.5 mg of ergonovine I felt within 30 minutes a not unpleasant inebriation characterized by hypnagogic visions and increased sensitivity to colors. After about three hours the effect had disappeared."

SOURCE 4 — Ruck on the policy implications (The Road to Eleusis, 1978):
"If the Mysteries were the greatest religious experience of the ancient world — and if they involved the ingestion of a psychoactive substance — then the right to that experience is not a marginal or exotic religious claim. It is the most classical religious claim in Western civilization."

SOURCE 5 — Modern Eleusis:
Modern Eleusis (Elefsina) is an industrial port city, site of one of the largest oil refineries in Greece. The ruins of the telesterion are visible adjacent to the refinery. Elefsina was named European Capital of Culture for 2023.

sourceEvidence:
SOURCE 1 — Rat Park (Chasing the Scream, Hari, 2015):
"The rats with good lives didn't like the drugged water. They mostly shunned it, consuming less than a quarter of the drugs the isolated rats used. None of them died. While all the rats who were alone and unhappy became heavy users, none of the rats who had a happy environment did."
"Professor Alexander argues that addiction is an adaptation. It's not you. It's your cage."

SOURCE 2 — Portugal (Chasing the Scream):
"In 2001, Portugal decriminalized all drugs — not just cannabis, but cocaine, heroin, everything. João Goulão, the architect of the policy, told me: 'We are dealing with people who have a health problem. Not criminals.'"
"By 2012, the number of people dying from street drug overdoses had fallen from eighty a year to just three. HIV infections among drug users had fallen by 95 percent."

SOURCE 3 — Integration as medicine (Labate & Cavnar, Ayahuasca Healing and Science, 2021):
"A consistent finding across ayahuasca studies for addiction and depression is that the experience is not sufficient by itself. Integration — the process of assimilating insights from the session into everyday life, through ongoing therapeutic support and community — determines outcomes at least as strongly as the pharmacological event itself."

SOURCE 4 — The opioid system and social bonding:
Social isolation activates the same neural pathways as physical pain. The opioid system, which is hijacked by heroin, is also the system that mediates social bonding. This is the same receptors — not a metaphor.

records.publisherRelationship: Independent RN Collins editorial prototype; no Fat Nugs affiliation, endorsement, sponsorship, ownership, or revenue relationship is asserted.
records.rightsBasis: original editorial or bibliographic/educational metadata; cited third-party sources are not reproduced wholesale
sourceEvidence:
SOURCE 1 — McKenna on machine elves:
"When you break through on DMT you are in the presence of the other. It is there. It's waiting. These entities are not formed like the usual objects of the visual world. They are more like the experience of self. They are, apparently, aware of you. They have an agenda. They want to communicate. They are giving you objects made of language, made of meaning. They are showing you that meaning can be made visible."

SOURCE 2 — Strassman's DMT studies (DMT: The Spirit Molecule, 2001):
"Many of our volunteers reported encounters with 'beings' or 'entities.' These beings often communicated specific information to subjects — information that subjects experienced as accurate and meaningful. The entities appeared to be aware of the subject's presence and interested in the subject's state of mind."

SOURCE 3 — The research literature (Timmermann et al., 2019 survey):
"Entity encounters were reported by the majority of survey respondents. Entities were described as autonomous, as having their own agenda, and as communicating information that subjects experienced as novel. Cross-cultural consistency in entity descriptions suggests the phenomenon is not solely a product of cultural expectation."

SOURCE 4 — The neurological framework (Nichols, 2016):
"Human beings show hyperactivated tendency toward agent detection — the attribution of intentionality to complex patterns — as an evolutionary adaptation. Psychedelics, by disrupting the default mode network's filtering function, may allow this agent-detection tendency to operate without its normal inhibitory constraints."

SOURCE 5 — The limitation:
The agent-detection framework cannot account for cases in which entities appear to convey accurate information that subjects did not bring into the session. Several of Strassman's subjects reported entities conveying specific details about their lives that were subsequently verified.

sourceEvidence:
SOURCE 1 — Popular Mechanics, February 1938:
"American farmers are promised a new cash crop with an annual value of several hundred million dollars, all because a machine has been invented which solves a problem almost as old as history. Hemp is the standard fiber of the world. It has great tensile strength and durability. It is used to produce more than 5,000 textile products."

SOURCE 2 — Anslinger's congressional testimony, 1937:
"There are 100,000 total marijuana smokers in the US and most are Negroes, Hispanics, Filipinos, and entertainers. Their Satanic music, jazz and swing, result from marijuana use. This marijuana causes white women to seek sexual relations with Negroes, entertainers, and any others."

SOURCE 3 — AMA opposition (congressional record, 1937):
"The American Medical Association knows of no evidence that marijuana is a dangerous drug." The AMA's Dr. William Woodward testified that the bill had been introduced without consultation with the medical profession and that the evidence presented was inadequate. His testimony was dismissed.

SOURCE 4 — Racial enforcement data (Marlan, Beyond Cannabis, 2019):
"Black Americans are arrested for cannabis possession at rates approximately four times higher than white Americans, despite similar usage rates, in states across the country. This disparity has persisted across decades of enforcement."

SOURCE 5 — Ehrlichman on Nixon (Dan Baum, 2016):
"We knew we couldn't make it illegal to be either against the war or black, but by getting the public to associate the hippies with marijuana and blacks with heroin, and then criminalizing both heavily, we could disrupt those communities." The account rests on Baum's notes alone, and Ehrlichman's family and several former Nixon aides dispute it.

sourceEvidence:
SOURCE 1 — María Sabina's verdict (Hofmann, LSD: My Problem Child, 1979):
When Hofmann gave María Sabina synthetic psilocybin pills, she used them in a healing ceremony. Afterward she said the pills lacked the spirit of the mushrooms, though by dawn she said they had the same power (Hofmann, LSD: My Problem Child, chapter 6).

SOURCE 2 — Gregoire on the industry (NEO.LIFE, 2020):
"Sabina's house was burned. Her son was murdered. She died in poverty in 1985. The psilocybin industry that her knowledge made possible is now worth $1.1 billion."
"The psychedelic drug market is projected to reach $6.85 billion by 2027."
"Journey Colab was the first psychedelic pharmaceutical company to pledge adherence to the Nagoya Protocol — the UN biodiversity agreement designed to prevent biopiracy."

SOURCE 3 — Schultes on indigenous knowledge (NIMH Symposium, 1967):
"Perhaps the greatest enemy of ethnopharmacological research is the arrival and cheap availability of the aspirin pill."
"In the search for new hallucinogens, we have much to do and little time in which to do it."

SOURCE 4 — The entourage effect (Labate & Cavnar, Therapeutic Use of Ayahuasca, 2014):
"The beta-carbolines in Banisteriopsis caapi not only inhibit the MAO enzymes that would otherwise metabolize DMT — harmine independently inhibits DYRK1A kinase, promoting neurogenesis through a mechanism entirely separate from the psychedelic effect. The whole plant produces effects that the isolated compound does not."

SOURCE 5 — LisaNa Macias Red Bear (Gregoire, 2020):
"We used this medicine before Jesus Christ walked this Earth."
